Good New Orleans website design starts with the fact that nobody here lives in "New Orleans." They live in the Marigny, Gentilly, Algiers or Uptown, they eat on Freret, they shop on Magazine, and they will tell you which side of Canal Street a place is on before they tell you its name. A visitor in town for a weekend searches the same way, because every guidebook taught them those names. A site that only says "serving the New Orleans area" is the one thing in this city that sounds like it came from nowhere.

Dominion Web Design Pro writes sites that use the real names. Maurice Johnson builds each one by hand from Big Sandy in East Texas, you see a free demo before any invoice, and the price is printed: $497, $997 or $1,997, one time.

Web design New Orleans visitors and neighbors both search by place

Orleans Parish and the City of New Orleans share the same boundary, and the Census Bureau put the population at about 362,000 in its July 2025 estimate. Inside that line are dozens of neighborhoods with names known well past Louisiana, and each one draws a different kind of searcher. The table is how we think about it when we plan a page.

Where you areWho is usually lookingWhat your page should answer first
French Quarter, Marigny, TremeVisitors on foot, many on their first tripExact block, hours tonight, whether to book, what it costs
Bywater, Mid-City, FreretLocals and repeat visitors hunting for something less touristyWhat makes you different, the menu or lineup, parking or the nearest streetcar line
Magazine Street and UptownShoppers working their way along a long streetWhich stretch you are on, what you carry, when you open
Gentilly, Algiers, New Orleans EastNeighbors who want a trade, a clinic or a caterer close to homeThe neighborhoods you serve, how to call, how quickly you can come
Metairie and the NorthshoreSuburban households who rarely type "New Orleans" at allTheir own town name, plainly, on a page written for it

Magazine Street shows why the detail matters. The city's tourism office describes it as about six miles long, running from Canal Street to Audubon Park through the Central Business District, the Garden District and Uptown, with locally owned shops as the rule. "On Magazine" tells a shopper almost nothing about where you are; a cross street and a neighborhood name tell them everything.

The jobs behind the plates and the stages

Hospitality is not a side industry here. Bureau of Labor Statistics data published through FRED counted about 69,400 leisure and hospitality jobs in the New Orleans metro in December 2025, and about 58,800 of them were in accommodation and food services alone. Against roughly 478,000 nonfarm jobs in the metro that month, that works out to about one job in seven. The annual average was 69,000 in 2024, up from about 53,900 in 2020.

Behind those numbers are thousands of owner-run operations: the po-boy counter, the second-line brass band, the walking tour guide with a ghost route, the jeweler selling at a weekend market, the caterer who cooks for weddings and office lunches. Most of them sell through word of mouth and a phone, and most have a website that was set up once by a cousin and never touched again.

Carnival, Jazz Fest and the weeks you get the most strangers

Carnival season opens on Twelfth Night, January 6, and Mardi Gras itself falls on Tuesday, February 9, 2027. The New Orleans Jazz and Heritage Festival is set for two long weekends at the Fair Grounds Race Course, April 22 to 25 and April 29 to May 2, 2027, with the lineup usually announced around December. Those weeks fill the city with people who have never walked past your door, and every one of them checks a phone first. If parades close your block, if you run a festival menu or if a band you book is playing a late set, the home page should say so weeks ahead, and your Google Business Profile should say the same thing.

A typical owner, walked through

Picture a made-up example, not a client: a two-person kitchen on Freret that does lunch, takes catering orders, and books a trio on Friday nights. Freret is a good place to imagine it. The National Trust's Main Street program adopted the corridor in 2001, and by 2011 local food writers were calling the blocks between Napoleon and Jefferson avenues the city's newest restaurant row.

  1. The menu goes on the page as text.Not a photo of a chalkboard. Typed dishes load fast on a phone, read clearly, and can be matched to a search for "shrimp po-boy Uptown."
  2. Catering gets its own page.How many people, how far ahead to order, delivery range by neighborhood, and a form that sends the request straight to the owner's email.
  3. Friday music has a short calendar.Date, start time, cover or no cover. The owner texts new dates, and we post them.
  4. Hours carry the exceptions.Parade days, summer closures, the Monday off. The site and the Google listing stay matched so nobody drives over to a locked door.

A tour guide, a brass band or a clinic Uptown would get a different list, but the method is the same: find out what the customer needs to decide, then put it where a thumb can reach it.

Web design New Orleans LA owners do not have to babysit

Not every New Orleans business sells po-boys. Dentists in Lakeview, therapists in Mid-City, roofers working the East and electricians crossing the river to Algiers all get searched the same way, by service and neighborhood. Google says local results depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. A page that names what you do and the parts of town you serve gives the first two a clear answer; nobody can promise a ranking, and we will not.

Here is what each package means for a business in the city. Starter, $497, is five hand-written pages including a service area page, live in 7 to 14 days, which suits a single shop or a solo musician. Pro, $997, adds a ten-page site with a photo gallery, local SEO with Google Business Profile setup, your Google reviews on the site, and ten city pages, which is the right size for a trade working Orleans, Jefferson and St. Tammany. Its AI chat widget is free for 14 days, then $297 a month. Agency, $1,997, starts with keyword research across your whole area, then writes a page for every town and service pair worth having, delivered in waves with the first live inside two weeks; it includes AI phone agent setup, and the agent is free for 7 days, then $297 a month for up to 750 minutes, cancel any time.

All three prices are paid once. Hosting, maintenance and updates are included while you keep the AI agent, or $49 a month without it. We do not sell page counts: a strong page for Metairie beats a hundred thin pages for every suburb on the map. Online stores with carts are not part of the packages, and we will tell you so before you buy.

Web design Louisiana owners can pair with free local help

A website is one tool. These groups help with the rest, and we have no tie to any of them.

LSBDC Greater New Orleans Region

The Louisiana Small Business Development Center network is hosted statewide by LSU through ten regional offices. The Greater New Orleans office is hosted by Xavier University of Louisiana and serves Orleans, Jefferson, Plaquemines, St. Bernard, St. Charles, St. James and St. John the Baptist parishes, with an office on North Causeway in Metairie.

New Orleans Chamber of Commerce

Founded in 2004, the chamber runs networking events, education and advocacy for its members, along with groups such as its Women's Business Alliance.

City Office of Supplier Diversity

For owners who want city contracts, this office certifies firms under the State and Local Disadvantaged Business Enterprise program, which is race and gender neutral. Applications go through an online system, and approved firms are listed in a public directory.

Propeller

A local nonprofit that in 2025 ran a Growth Accelerator for 15 growth-stage entrepreneurs from May to July and a Startup Bootcamp from September to November, and leads a Financial Wellness Collaborative with Thrive New Orleans and Fund 17.

Common questions

How much does New Orleans website design cost for a small business?

Quotes around town run from a few hundred dollars to many thousands, and many firms only give a number after a meeting. Ours are printed and paid once: Starter is $497 for five hand-written pages, Pro is $997 for ten pages plus ten researched city pages, and Agency is $1,997 for a page for every town and service pair worth targeting. Hosting, maintenance and updates are $49 a month, or included while you keep the AI agent.

Do you build websites for musicians and bands in New Orleans?

Yes, as long as what you need is a clear site and not an online store. A working musician usually needs a short bio, a list of upcoming gigs with venue and time, a booking form for weddings and private events, and links to where people can hear you. You send new dates and we post them as part of maintenance.

Can one site cover New Orleans, Metairie and the Northshore?

It can, and it should if you really work all three. Customers in Metairie or on the Northshore search with their own town names, so a single page that says "Greater New Orleans" helps no one. The Pro package includes ten city pages, each researched and written for that place, and Agency starts with keyword research across your whole area to decide which towns earn a page.

Should my website change during Mardi Gras or Jazz Fest?

Usually, yes. If parades change your hours, close your street or bring a special menu, put that on the home page a few weeks ahead and match it on your Google Business Profile. Visitors plan from their phones, often from another city, and the site is the only thing they can check. We make those updates for you.

Is there a web design company with an office in New Orleans behind this page?

No. Dominion Web Design Pro is Maurice Johnson in Big Sandy, East Texas, and he builds every site remotely. Call (903) 636-7511 any hour: an AI receptionist answers and can transfer you to Maurice.

Want to see your New Orleans site before you spend a dollar?

Give us your business name and what you do, and a demo site gets built for you to look at on your own phone. If you like it, pick a package. If you do not, you have spent nothing but the minute it took to look.
